subtype: Easy credit and buy now pay later [Actor]
passage:
Day 1. The banner said "no-cost EMI" and Kashish felt lucky. A 48,000-rupee laptop became 4,000 a month, which barely felt like money. Her friend Pranav asked, "Do you need it?" She shrugged. "It's basically free." She tapped buy, then added earbuds on one instalment plan and a jacket on another.

Day 40. Three reminders arrived in one week. She missed a date by two days and a late fee appeared. The amount owed on her phone looked much heavier than each small instalment had ever felt.

Day 75. At Pranav's suggestion she wrote all three plans on one page: total owed, dates, fees. She paid the smallest plan first, stopped tapping "pay later" and made a rule to wait three days before any instalment purchase.

qa.q: What did the banner offer that made Kashish feel lucky?
qa.a: The banner offered no-cost EMI, which turned a 48,000-rupee laptop into 4,000 a month.

qa.q: What did Kashish think about the instalments when she shrugged and said it was basically free?
qa.a: Kashish felt lucky and relaxed, believing small monthly amounts were hardly real money.

qa.q: What turning point on Day 75 helped Kashish get control?
qa.a: She wrote all three plans on one page with total owed, dates and fees, paid the smallest first and made a three-day waiting rule.

qa.q: How did Pranav's question on Day 1 show a different view from Kashish's?
qa.a: Pranav asked whether Kashish needed the laptop, treating it as a real purchase, while Kashish saw it as basically free.

grounding: Shows a young adult treating instalment and pay-later offers as free money until small payments, a late fee and a growing total show the trap.

subtype: Easy credit and buy now pay later [Actor]
passage: Bhavna, come sit. Yes, I saw the phone on the table, and no, I am not scolding. I'm Arohi, your masi, and at twenty-one I was you. A stall at our college fair handed me a card with no joining fee. I bought a music system, two dresses and a watch, paying only the minimum each month. Within a year what I owed had grown by half, and late charges piled on top. My father found the letter and said nothing all evening. Then he sat beside me with a sheet of paper and made me write the full total, every charge, every date. I paid the biggest charge first and took extra tuition classes for eight months to clear the rest. Read the total, Bhavna, not the monthly number.

qa.q: What did the stall at the college fair hand Arohi?
qa.a: It handed Arohi a card with no joining fee.

qa.q: Why did Arohi keep buying things on the card at twenty-one?
qa.a: Arohi felt confident and free, because paying only the minimum each month seemed to mean paying little.

qa.q: What turning point helped Arohi start clearing the debt?
qa.a: Writing the full total, every charge and every date on paper, then paying the biggest charge first.

qa.q: What did Arohi's father's silence, and then sitting beside her with paper, show about how he felt?
qa.a: It showed he was worried but wanted to help, so he stayed calm and helped Arohi face the real numbers.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how card offers and minimum payments hid a growing total and late charges.
